identification.summary: China-based cyber-espionage actor that Microsoft tracks as Swirl Typhoon and maps to TELLURIUM, STALKER PANDA, Tick, Bronze Butler and REDBALDKNIGHT [S1]. Unit 42 describes Tick as primarily targeting organizations in Japan and the Republic of Korea [S8]. Recent reporting covers a 2021-2022 supply-chain compromise of an East Asian data-loss-prevention (DLP) vendor [S5] and mid-2025 zero-day exploitation of Motex LANSCOPE Endpoint Manager (CVE-2025-61932) [S3][S4].
identification.firstObserved: Trend Micro says it has tracked the group since 2008 [S9].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Swirl Typhoon; Microsoft's mapping lists TELLURIUM, STALKER PANDA, Tick, Bronze Butler and REDBALDKNIGHT as other names [S1]. Stalker Taurus (Unit 42) appears in this record's imported aliases but was not confirmed in sources gathered here. MITRE tracks the group as BRONZE BUTLER (G0060) [S12]. 'PLA Unit 61419' is a Japanese government attribution of sponsorship, not a vendor cluster name [S10][S11].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China. In April 2021, Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary Katsunobu Kato said one of the suspected attackers worked for People's Liberation Army Unit 61419, which is sometimes called Tick [S10]. The National Police Agency's Mitsuhiro Matsumoto said it was highly likely that PLA Unit 61419, a strategic support unit operating from Qingdao, Shandong, was involved [S11].
attribution.confidence: Japanese government officials named PLA Unit 61419 as highly likely involved [S10][S11]. Recorded Future's Insikt Group told The Record the unit-level attribution was most likely based on older Chinese military intelligence collected before recent PLA reforms [S11]. ESET attributed the DLP-vendor compromise to Tick with high confidence [S5]. China rejected the Japanese allegations [S11].
attribution.basis: Japanese police investigation of the 2016 JAXA intrusions, including a case filed against a Chinese national who allegedly rented servers used in the attacks while living in Japan [S10]; vendor malware and infrastructure analysis by Sophos, Unit 42, Trend Micro and ESET [S3][S5][S8][S9].

objectives: Long-term espionage. Trend Micro reported attempts to steal military-related documents from defense firms [S9]. ESET judged cyberespionage the most likely aim of the DLP-vendor compromise, whose customers include government and military bodies [S5]. Sophos said the 2025 LANSCOPE targeting appeared limited to sectors aligned with the group's intelligence objectives [S3][S4].

sectors: Defense, aerospace, chemical and satellite firms [S9]
Government and military customers of a DLP software vendor (supply chain) [S5]
Air-gapped critical systems via South Korean secure USB drives [S8]
regions: East Asia (DLP vendor and its customers) [S5]
Japanese firms with subsidiaries in China [S9]
targeting.notes: Japanese investigators linked the campaign to roughly 200 Japanese companies and research bodies, but JAXA was the only victim publicly named [S10][S11]. Imported actor summary also lists Taiwan, Hong Kong and the United States; no source gathered here confirmed those regions.

capabilities.summary: Zero-day exploitation, including a 2016 zero-day in the Japanese asset-management product SKYSEA Client View [S3] and mid-2025 zero-day exploitation of LANSCOPE Endpoint Manager CVE-2025-61932, which lets unauthenticated attackers run code with SYSTEM privileges [S3][S4][S13]. Supply-chain operations: compromise of a DLP vendor's internal update servers and trojanized third-party tool installers (Q-Dir) passed to customers [S5]. Weaponized secure USB drives aimed at air-gapped systems [S8]. Use of hijacked legitimate email accounts and credentials to deliver malware [S9]. Custom malware families include Daserf [S12], Minzen, Datper, Nioupale and HomamDownloader [S8], ShadowPy, Netboy and Ghostdown [S5], and the Gokcpdoor proxy backdoor, with the Havoc C2 framework used in some 2025 intrusions [S4].

campaigns.name: Weaponized secure USB drives
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 reports Tick loaded malicious files onto a South Korean defense company's secure USB drives, likely to reach air-gapped systems.

campaigns.name: Operation ENDTRADE
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro reports multi-stage backdoors used against Japanese defense, aerospace, chemical and satellite firms, including attempted theft of military-related documents.

campaigns.name: DLP software vendor supply-chain compromise
campaigns.summary: ESET reports Tick compromised an East Asian DLP vendor's update servers from March 2021, then passed trojanized Q-Dir installers to customers in February and June 2022.

campaigns.name: LANSCOPE Endpoint Manager zero-day (CVE-2025-61932)
campaigns.summary: Sophos CTU observed BRONZE BUTLER exploiting the flaw before a patch to deploy Gokcpdoor; Motex released fixes on 2025-10-20 and CISA added the CVE to its KEV catalog.

diamond.adversary: China-based operators; Japan's government names PLA Unit 61419 as highly likely involved [S10][S11].
diamond.capability: Zero-day exploitation of Japanese endpoint and asset-management software, supply-chain trojanizing, weaponized USB drives, and custom backdoors such as Datper, ShadowPy, Netboy and Gokcpdoor [S3][S4][S5][S8].
diamond.infrastructure: A compromised vendor's update servers [S5]; servers rented by a suspect while in Japan (per Japanese police) [S10]; hijacked legitimate email accounts [S9]; Gokcpdoor proxy C2 and Havoc C2 [S4].
diamond.victim: Japanese defense, aerospace, chemical and satellite firms; JAXA; South Korean organizations; government and military customers of an East Asian DLP vendor [S5][S8][S9][S10].
diamond.socioPolitical: PRC intelligence collection on its regional rival Japan and on Korean defense, including military-related documents and space-agency data [S9][S10].
diamond.technology: Trust in locally popular Japanese endpoint-management software (LANSCOPE, SKYSEA), vendor update channels, remote support tools and certified secure USB media [S3][S5][S8].

gaps: Primary vendor reports could not be opened (Sophos, ESET, Unit 42, The Register, The Record and The Hacker News were unreachable from this environment); claims rely on search-result summaries of those pages.
Exact publication dates for the Sophos LANSCOPE blog, BleepingComputer article, The Record article and the Unit 42 USB report were not confirmed in search results; month-level dates are given.
No Microsoft Threat Intelligence report naming Swirl Typhoon activity was found; Microsoft's mapping is the only Microsoft source.
The PLA Unit 61419 attribution comes from Japanese officials; Recorded Future questions whether it reflects the post-reform PLA structure. No US government attribution was located.
Initial access for the DLP-vendor compromise is unknown, per ESET coverage.
The number of compromised secure USB drives is unknown, per Unit 42.
Imported summary mentions ties to China's National University of Defense Technology and targeting of Taiwan, Hong Kong and the US; not verified in sources gathered.
ShadowPad appears in MITRE's software list for G0060 and AhnLab has linked Tick to 'Operation Triple Tiang' (Korea); neither was reviewed here.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain includes region-specific endpoint and asset-management servers (LANSCOPE, SKYSEA), software vendors' update and remote-support channels, and removable-media workflows into air-gapped networks at Japanese and Korean defense partners [S3][S5][S8]. STEP 2: Zero-day exploitation of on-premises management software and supply-chain trojanizing shrink warning time; air-gap assumptions do not hold where certified USB media is trusted [S3][S5][S8]. STEP 3: Doctrinal template: access through an exploited management agent, a trojanized installer, a spearphish from a hijacked partner mailbox; then a downloader and a custom backdoor (Gokcpdoor, Netboy, Datper), followed by collection of military-related documents [S4][S5][S9]. STEP 4: MLCOA: continued espionage against Japanese defense-industrial and government-adjacent organizations through zero-days in locally popular enterprise software. MDCOA: compromise of a security or management vendor serving the Japan Self-Defense Forces or US forces in Japan, used to push malware across many enclaves at once, including air-gapped systems. Candidate indicators: inbound traffic to LANSCOPE agent ports from untrusted hosts; Gokcpdoor listeners (Sophos noted ports 38000 and 38002); unexpected Q-Dir or utility installers delivered through vendor support sessions; Havoc C2 beacons [S3][S4][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track Japanese- and Korean-specific software in partner and host-nation networks, since this actor exploits products US vulnerability feeds may cover late; CISA KEV listed CVE-2025-61932 only after Motex's October 2025 fix [S3][S13]. (2) Authorities: activity mainly affects allied and host-nation systems, so response relies on coordination with Japanese authorities (NPA, JPCERT/CC) rather than unilateral US action [S10]. (3) Mission assurance: treat removable media and vendor update/remote-support paths into mission and air-gapped systems as attack surface [S5][S8]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with DIB partners that have Japanese subsidiaries or suppliers, since Trend Micro saw targeting of Japanese firms with subsidiaries in China and of defense suppliers [S9].

provenance.importedSummary: Tick is a cyber espionage group with likely Chinese origins that has been active since at least 2008. The group appears to have close ties to the Chinese National University of Defense and Technology, which is possibly linked to the PLA. This threat actor targets organizations in the critical infrastructure, heavy industry, manufacturing, and international relations sectors for espionage purposes. The attacks appear to be centered on political, media, and engineering sectors. STALKER PANDA has been observed conducting targeted attacks against Japan, Taiwan, Hong Kong, and the United States.
